A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same modular sentence-encoder research. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support matching retained content despite substantial revisions to the method and experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original STS/STR and Belebele question-answering experiments, including detailed LaBSE and Glot500 results and alignment ablations in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original LaBSE and mE5 experiments on similarity, relatedness, classification and bitext mining, plus alignment diagnostics and component ablations. Appendix D supplies detailed results.

M1.justification: V1 fully tunes monolingual encoders and trains CLA adapters only on paraphrases. V2 uses language-specific embeddings and separate LoRA language and sentence-encoding adapters with frozen earlier components. Its joint CLA training alternates paraphrase batches using MNRL with parallel batches using cosine-similarity loss (Section 3 and Appendix B). These substantially change the architecture and training procedure.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 23-language pool and five core paraphrase-training corpora, but removes STS22 news-article similarity and Belebele MCQA. It adds multilingual SICK relatedness, FLORES/Tatoeba bitext mining and SIB-200 classification, and expands cross-lingual STS pairs. K-STS is retained under STSB, with additional Korean cross-language pairs; it is not simply deleted.

E2.justification: The evaluated SONAR, Glot500 and mE5-large comparisons in v1 disappear. V2 retains LaBSE and mE5-base and adds English-only Full_en and Mod_en controls (Tables 1–2). The earlier Single_m, Single_c and Single_mc baselines correspond to Full_m, Full_c and Full_mc; their renaming alone is not a comparator addition.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes LaBSE baseline training from one to three epochs, language adaptation from 100K to 200K steps, and the tokenizer-training cap from 5M to 10M sentences. CLA batch size changes from 128 to 256 and learning rate from 1e-4 to 2e-5. New evaluation procedures include frozen-encoder logistic regression, bitext xsim scores, pooled multilingual language-bias evaluation and RSIM.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit removal ablations for language adaptation and monolingual SE training, comparisons of paraphrase-only, parallel-only and joint alignment, and language-bias/RSIM analyses. The English-pivot versus all-pair experiment is retained but redesigned for seven STSB languages and both alignment objectives. V1's larger-English-data experiment and independently initialized BERT/BERTbek alignment check are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests for its experiments. Both present point estimates and averages across languages rather than statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive classification, mining, SICK, diagnostic and ablation results, while removing STS22, Belebele, SONAR and Glot500 result blocks. For example, its new trained-mE5 comparison reports cross-lingual STSB correlations of 73.8 for Mod_mc-jt and 66.7 for Full_mc (Tables 2 and 10). LaBSE results are also revised, but changed training and language-pair coverage prevent treating them as clean same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results or proofs. V2's descriptions of adopted language-bias and RSIM measures specify empirical evaluation procedures; they do not add substantive mathematical theory or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution from separating monolingual specialization and cross-lingual alignment to also addressing conflicting requirements among cross-lingual tasks. V2 claims balanced performance through joint paraphrase/parallel training, supported by mining and classification evaluations, and explicitly emphasizes improvements over full-parameter training rather than pursuing state-of-the-art performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting classification performance with isomorphism and lexical cues, and explains the differing effects of paraphrase and parallel alignment. Its efficiency discussion replaces v1's proposed future use of parameter-efficient specialization with remaining module and vocabulary costs. The limitations newly state that encoder-decoder MSEs require adaptations before the approach can be applied.

D1.justification: The reproduction recipe is substantially revised: v2 documents separate LoRA placements, rank 8, alpha 16, dropout 0.1 and training precision, and adds per-module parameter sizes and timings in Table 4. The model-access inventory and first-page code pointer change. Conversely, v1's explicit MLM sequence length and training-script link are no longer supplied.

R1.justification: V1 primarily positions the work around monolingual specialization, fine-grained semantics and differences from LASER3. V2 substantially expands discussion of language-disentanglement and lightweight multilingual-adapter research, including Mao et al., Liu et al. and Yano et al., and claims novelty in jointly addressing conflicting MSE requirements. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method and results discussion are extensively rewritten. V2 introduces numbered method/setup subsections, separates Results from Discussion, consolidates detailed evaluation reporting in Appendix D, and changes Single/Multi terminology to Full/Mod. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show individual LoRA modules, trainable components and alternating alignment batches; v1's Belebele bar chart is removed. Main results are reorganized into broad task-and-diagnostic summary Tables 1–2, with extensive language-level tables in Appendix D. V2 also adds the module-size/training-time table, substantially changing the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves parameter-efficient monolingual specialization as future work and lacks direct ablations separating language adaptation from SE training. V2 implements that specialization and adds those ablations on LaBSE and mE5, alongside direct alignment diagnostics, substantially strengthening the central methodological argument. Removing STS22/Belebele and initialization/data ablations narrows some evidence, and v2's mE5 Mod_m SICK mean is inconsistent between Table 2 (75.4) and Table 12 (76.3). These drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger component validation and clearer account of task trade-offs.
